extracted.intended_audience: educators, policymakers, and general readers interested in scientific method, science education, and the role of science in citizenship
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what counts as 'good science' and for evaluating popular scientific writing, emphasizing scientific method, classification of facts, and the educational/moral role of science in citizenship. Includes guidance on distinguishing good science from bad popularisation, metaphysics, or philosophical speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as training in method for citizenship
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Science, as training the mind to an exact and impartial analysis of 'facts', is an education specially fitted to promote sound citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate science (and its instruction) by its effectiveness in forming minds that analyse facts impartially and hence contribute to 'more efficient citizenship' and social stability. The social justification of science is not only utilitarian knowledge but the moral/educational outcome in conduct (citizens less prone to emotional or partisan decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of facts and formation of unbiased judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification of facts, the recognition of their sequence and relative significance, and the formation of judgments upon these facts unbiassed by personal feeling is characteristic of the scientific frame of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific account should show clear classification of data and derive conclusions from that classification; it should strive at 'self-elimination' of the author's idiosyncrasies so conclusions are as true for others as for the author. Assessors should look for explicit treatment of facts, sequences, and the logical steps to conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and unity of science: method over material
rubrics_metrics.description: The unity of all science consists alone in its method, not in its material; the field of science is unlimited because any classified facts and their sequences become material for science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a work, prioritize whether it applies scientific method (orderly classification, recognition of relationships and recurring sequences) rather than focusing on the novelty of its subject-matter. The method's applicability across domains (physical, social, historical) is itself a criterion of scientific validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method applicable to social as well as physical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method of examining facts is not peculiar to one class of phenomena and to one class of workers; it is applicable to social as well as to physical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social-science or applied works by the same standards used for natural science: clear classification of facts, recognition of relationships and sequences, and minimization of personal bias. Guard against dismissing social treatments as non-scientific merely because their subject-matter differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good popular science must teach method, not merely facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The first aim of any genuine work of science, however popular, ought to be the presentation of such a classification of facts that the reader's mind is irresistibly led to acknowledge a logical sequence — a law which appeals to the reason before it captivates the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing popular science writing, reject works that 'merely recite the results of investigations' or that appeal primarily to imagination. Prefer texts that expose the classificatory framework and logical progression leading to conclusions. Use this as a test for 'bad science' vs 'good science' popularisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad science: conclusions not flowing from facts or unstated assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we come across a conclusion in a scientific work which does not flow from the classification of facts, or which is not directly stated by the author to be an assumption, then we are dealing with bad science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect arguments for whether conclusions are derived from presented classifications/evidence or are asserted without basis. Penalize works that conceal assumptions or present imaginative/speculative claims as established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and intelligibility: scientific works should be accessible to logical minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Good science will always be intelligible to the logically trained mind, if that mind can read and translate the language in which science is written; classics often more intelligible than popularisations by those with less insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity and rigor of exposition: is the terminology used consistently? Is sufficient interpretive guidance provided for non-specialists? Prefer works that sacrifice rhetorical flourish for precise, learnable scientific language and that enable readers to trace argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction should emphasize method over mere accumulation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The true aim of the teacher must be to impart an appreciation of method and not a knowledge of facts; concentrating on a small range of phenomena better imparts method than superficial surveys of wide fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating curricula, courses, or outreach, prefer programs that give students hands-on or deep exposure to a limited set of phenomena to cultivate the habit of classification and reasoning. Criticize educational schemes (or polytechnic instruction) that emphasize manual/technical instruction without accompanying pure-science method.

rubrics_metrics.name: No short cuts to truth; honesty about ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no short cut to truth, no way to gain a knowledge of the universe except through the gateway of scientific method; where science is ignorant it should frankly confess ignorance rather than claim a different relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging claims, penalize appeals to 'short and easy cuts' or proclamations that some domains lie beyond scientific method. Reward authors who acknowledge limits of current knowledge and avoid erecting speculative preserves immune to empirical test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphysics and speculative systems must be grounded in facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Either metaphysics are based on an accurate classification of facts, or they are not; if not, metaphysics are built on air or quicksands and produce divergent proprietary systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metaphysical or grand-theory claims skeptically unless they demonstrate accurate empirical classification and show that different investigators would reach similar judgments. Identify as problematic any system that excludes or contradicts empirical findings or other investigators' results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method contrasted: beware internal-cogitation-only approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophical method seems based upon an analysis which does not start with the classification of facts, but reaches its judgments by some obscure process of internal cogitation, and is therefore dangerously liable to influence of individual bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate philosophical or conceptual treatments by checking whether they begin from empirical classification and whether they yield practical unanimity among different investigators. Penalize approaches that rely on untested introspective argumentation and that generate endless competing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific works should lead to practical agreement among investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Though physicists or biologists may differ in measurements or hypotheses, yet in the fundamental principles and sequences the professors of each individual science are in practical agreement among themselves; the scientific method tends toward practical unanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concordance among independent investigators as an indicator: a robust scientific treatment should be reproducible and, when facts are properly classified, should produce agreement in principle across competent readers. Low reproducibility or strong persistent disagreement signals weak classification or bias.
